entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: A polite way to say that you have a different opinion, without saying that the other person is wrong.
entries.usage: Useful in meetings, discussions and personal conversations when you want to disagree calmly. It focuses on your own view instead of attacking theirs, so it sounds respectful, often after a short acknowledgment like *I understand your point, but*. Explain your view right after, or it can sound as if you are ending the discussion.
examples: I know you think the move will be easy on the kids, but **I see it differently**.
"The movie was way too long." "Hmm, **I see it differently**. I thought every scene mattered."
My sister thinks our parents spoiled me, but **I see it differently**: they were just tired by the time I came along.

drill.sentence: "Homework is a waste of time for little kids." "I get that, but {{I see it differently}}. It teaches them good habits."
drill.hint: my opinion is not the same as yours; four words (not *I don't agree* or *I beg to differ*)

entries.related: *I don't see it that way* — same, a bit more direct; *I beg to differ* — formal or ironic; *I disagree* — plain and direct.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Says that you still have doubts and have not been persuaded that something is true, good or will work.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, discussions and personal decisions; it expresses polite but clear doubt and invites better reasons. It is used alone or with a *that*-clause or *by* + noun: *I'm not convinced (that) it'll work*, *I'm still not convinced by his story.*
examples: The salesman says this car will run for twenty years, but **I'm not convinced**.
"The new diet really works." "**I'm not convinced**. You've tried five diets this year."
The city says the new bridge is safe, but many residents **aren't convinced**.

drill.sentence: Everyone says the show gets better in season two, but {{I'm not convinced}}. The first season put me to sleep.
drill.hint: their claims haven't persuaded me (not *I'm not sure*, *I doubt it* or *I don't buy it*)

entries.related: *I'm not sure* — milder, less clear doubt; *I don't buy it* — casual, you don't believe it; *I have my doubts* — similar, a bit more formal.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Admits that the other person's view may be correct, while showing that you are still not completely sure.
entries.usage: A polite, open reply in discussions at work and at home; it lowers tension without fully giving in, and it is often followed by *but* and your remaining doubt. Said with a sigh, it can mean you are starting to accept something you didn't want to believe.
examples: "I bet the restaurant's closed on Mondays." "**You could be right**. Let me check online."
**You could be right** about the car — that noise might be the brakes.
"I think she's just shy, not rude." "Hmm, **you could be right**."

drill.sentence: "I think the cat's been eating your plants." "{{You could be right}}. That would explain the leaves on the floor."
drill.hint: maybe you're correct, but I'm not sure (not *you might …* or *you may …*)

entries.related: *you might be right* — same; *you have a point* — accepts one argument; *you're right* — full agreement.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Politely disagrees with how someone has described a person or situation, suggesting that the description is too strong or not accurate.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and meetings; *would* makes the disagreement sound soft and tentative. It is often followed by a better description: *I wouldn't say he's lazy — he's just tired.* It is also a modest reply to praise.
examples: "Your brother is so rude." "**I wouldn't say that**. He's just very direct."
"You must be rich now." "Ha, **I wouldn't say that**. The new job pays okay."
**I wouldn't say** the hotel was bad, but it wasn't worth three hundred dollars a night.

drill.sentence: "You're a professional photographer, right?" "Oh, {{I wouldn't say that}}. It's just a hobby."
drill.hint: modestly rejecting the description; four words (not *not really*)

entries.related: *not really* — short, casual; *that's a bit of a stretch* — the description goes too far; *I'm not sure about that* — doubts a claim.

entries.term: I hate to say it, but …
entries.spoken_term: I hate to say it, but
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces an unwelcome truth or opinion that the listener may not want to hear.
entries.usage: Common among friends, family and colleagues before bad news, criticism or an admission. It shows that you are not happy to say it, which softens it a little, but in *I hate to say it, but I told you so* it can sound smug. *I hate to break it to you* is for disappointing news.
examples: **I hate to say it, but** I think your car needs a new transmission.
We were lost for an hour, and **I hate to say it, but** Dad's paper map beat my phone.
"How's my cooking?" "**I hate to say it, but** the chicken's a little dry."

drill.sentence: {{I hate to say it, but}} I don't think our team has any chance of making the playoffs this year.
drill.hint: this is unpleasant to admit; six words before the truth (not *to be honest* or *I'm sorry to say*)

entries.related: *I hate to break it to you* — for disappointing news; *to be honest* — introduces a frank opinion; *I'm sorry to say* — more formal regret.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: A polite way to say that a statement is partly wrong or too simple, without calling it completely false.
entries.usage: Common in discussions, meetings, interviews and family arguments when you want to correct someone carefully, usually followed by the correction. It sounds more diplomatic than *That's wrong* or *That's not true*. *That's not quite right* is similar.
examples: "You never help with the dishes." "**That's not entirely true**. I did them on Sunday."
People say cats don't care about their owners, but **that's not entirely true**.
"The store doesn't take returns." "Well, **that's not entirely true** — they give store credit."

drill.sentence: "Everyone says the city's dangerous at night." "{{That's not entirely true}}. Most neighborhoods are perfectly safe."
drill.hint: polite: only partly false (not *… quite right*, *… necessarily …*, *… exactly …* or *… completely …*)

entries.related: *that's not quite right* — similar, for small errors; *that's not true* — direct denial; *not exactly* — casual, the statement is off.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Means *almost, but not completely*: something is close to being true, right or finished, but it isn't.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing, before an adjective, verb or noun (*not quite ready*, *not quite what I meant*), and as a short reply. As a reply it is softer than a plain *no*, so it is a polite way to correct someone.
examples: The cake's **not quite** done. Give it another five minutes.
"So you're from Boston?" "**Not quite**. I grew up about an hour north."
The new apartment is **not quite** what we'd hoped for, but it's close to work.

drill.sentence: "Is the paint dry yet?" "{{Not quite}}. Don't touch the door for another hour."
drill.hint: nearly, but not completely; two words (not *not yet* or *almost*)

entries.related: *not yet* — it will happen later; *almost* — very close; *not exactly* — polite or ironic correction.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: A polite *no*, used especially to answer *Do you mind …?* or *Would you mind …?*, meaning that it is no problem.
entries.usage: Common in polite conversation with strangers, colleagues and guests. After *Do you mind if I sit here?*, *Not at all* means *Please do*, because the question asks whether it bothers you. As a reply to *thank you* it is more common in British English; Americans usually say *No problem* or *You're welcome*.
examples: "Do you mind if I sit here?" "**Not at all**. Go ahead."
"Would you mind holding the door?" "**Not at all**."
"I hope I'm not bothering you." "Oh, **not at all** — come on in."

drill.sentence: "Would you mind if we pushed dinner back to eight?" "{{Not at all}}. That actually works better for me."
drill.hint: polite answer meaning it's no trouble; three words (not *no problem* or *of course not*)

mistake.wrong: "Do you mind if I open the window?" "Yes, go ahead."
mistake.right: "Do you mind if I open the window?" "Not at all, go ahead."
mistake.why: *Do you mind …?* asks whether it bothers you, so the polite permission is a *no*: *Not at all* or *No, go ahead*.

entries.related: *of course not* — same reply to *Do you mind …?*; *go ahead* — gives permission; *no problem* — the usual American reply to thanks.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: Checks what someone means, or challenges a remark that seems to suggest something unpleasant.
entries.usage: Common in discussions and arguments, followed by a clause: *Are you saying I'm wrong?* With a neutral tone it simply checks understanding, but with a sharp tone it sounds defensive, as if you heard an insult. *So what you're saying is …* is a calmer way to check meaning.
examples: **Are you saying** we need to cancel the whole trip, or just the first day?
"Maybe someone else should cook this year." "Wait — **are you saying** my turkey was bad?"
**Are you saying** the store won't refund me even with a receipt?

drill.sentence: "You might want to practice a little more before the recital." "{{Are you saying}} I'm not ready?"
drill.hint: checking a remark that sounds like criticism; three words (not *do you mean* or *you think*)

entries.related: *do you mean …?* — neutral check; *what are you trying to say?* — more suspicious; *what's that supposed to mean?* — offended.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Shows sudden confusion or shock at something you just heard, as if you need it repeated or explained.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech and texting, especially among younger people, as a quick reaction with a rise on *what*. It sounds surprised rather than rude, but it is too casual for formal situations. It is often used humorously when someone mentions big news very casually.
examples: "By the way, I quit my job yesterday." "**Wait, what?**"
"So after Jen and Mike got divorced…" "**Wait, what?** They got divorced?"
**Wait, what?** The concert's tonight? I thought it was next week!

drill.sentence: "Oh, and I sold the house." "{{Wait, what}}? You never told me you were selling!"
drill.hint: two words of shocked confusion (not *excuse me* or *sorry, …*)

entries.related: *hold on* — asks someone to stop and explain; *what?!* — plain shock; *excuse me?* — offended, not just surprised.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Said with a sharp rise in pitch when someone's remark surprises or offends you, meaning *Did you really just say that?*
entries.usage: Common in tense moments at home, in stores or at work; it signals that the remark was rude and gives the speaker a chance to take it back. With a polite, neutral tone, the same words can simply mean you didn't hear. Tone and facial expression make the difference.
examples: "Have you put on a few pounds?" "**Excuse me?**"
"Calm down, sweetheart." "**Excuse me?** Don't call me sweetheart."
When the guy in line told her to smile more, she just said, "**Excuse me?**"

drill.sentence: "Wow, you actually cleaned your room for once." "{{Excuse me}}? I clean it every week!"
drill.hint: offended reaction with rising pitch; two words (not *pardon me* or *say what*)

entries.related: *pardon me?* — mostly for not hearing; *I beg your pardon?* — formal, offended; *what's that supposed to mean?* — asks about a hidden insult.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: Invites someone to continue speaking after an interruption, often one that you caused.
entries.usage: Polite and common in conversations, meetings and phone calls, for example after your phone rings or two people start talking at once. It shows that you care about what they were saying. Without *sorry*, *You were saying?* can be ironic, said after events have just proved someone wrong.
examples: Ugh, that was the delivery guy. **Sorry, you were saying?**
"Oops, we both started talking at once." "Ha, yeah. **Sorry, you were saying?**"
The waiter finally left with our order, and I turned back to Dan: "**Sorry, you were saying?**"

drill.sentence: "And then the mechanic told us…" "Hold on, my dog's barking at someone. Okay, {{sorry, you were saying}}?"
drill.hint: asking her to continue after the interruption; four words (not *… go ahead* or *… go on*)

entries.related: *go on* — continue, short; *where were we?* — finds the topic again; *as I was saying* — the speaker returns to their own point.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you will say something again in different words, because it was unclear or came out wrong.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, interviews, classes and conversation, especially after a remark that sounded rude or confusing. It is a quick, polite way to correct yourself, often with a little laugh. *Let me put it another way* is more about explaining better than about fixing an awkward remark.
examples: You look great for your age. Wait, **let me rephrase that**. You look great, period.
Hmm, that came out wrong. **Let me rephrase that**.
"So you think my idea is bad?" "No, no, **let me rephrase that** — I think it needs more time."

drill.sentence: "Your sister is the smart one." "Wow." "Okay, {{let me rephrase that}}. You're both smart in different ways."
drill.hint: I'll say it again in other words (not *… put it another way* or *… try … again*)

entries.related: *let me put it another way* — explains differently; *that came out wrong* — admits an awkward remark; *what I meant was* — corrects what you said.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: Asks someone to repeat information that they already told you, such as a name or an address, because you have forgotten it.
entries.usage: Very common in casual and work conversations: *What was your name again?* The past tense *was* and *again* at the end show that you were told before, which makes the question polite and a little apologetic. Other verbs work too: *Where did you say you work again?*
entries.pattern: What was + noun + again? / Wh- question + again?
examples: I'm so sorry — **what was** your name **again**?
**What was** the address of the restaurant **again**? I'm already in the car.
Remind me, **what was** the name of that movie with the talking dog **again**?

drill.sentence: "I'll see you at the party tonight." "Great. {{What was the address again}}? I forgot to write it down."
drill.hint: ask her to repeat the location she told you before; five words, past tense

entries.related: *remind me …* — a polite way to ask the same thing; *sorry, I didn't catch …* — you didn't hear it the first time; *could you repeat that?* — neutral request.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces your personal opinion or impression: *in my opinion* or *the way I see it*.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, at the start of a sentence with a comma: *To me, it tastes like soap.* It marks the view as personal, so it sounds modest and makes disagreement easy. It also follows *seem*, *look* and *sound*: *That looks fine to me.*
examples: **To me**, the second apartment felt much brighter, even if it's smaller.
Everyone loves that show, but **to me** it's kind of boring.
"Is this shirt too bright?" "It looks fine **to me**."

drill.sentence: My friends think pineapple on pizza is gross, but {{to me}}, it's the perfect combination.
drill.hint: in my personal opinion; two words (not *for me*)

mistake.wrong: Your plan sounds strange for me.
mistake.right: Your plan sounds strange to me.
mistake.why: After *seem*, *sound* and *look*, the person who has the impression takes *to*, not *for*.

entries.related: *for me* — for preferences and effects on you (*It's too spicy for me*); *personally* — stresses that it's your own view; *in my opinion* — more formal.

entries.label: hedging phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you think something is true or will happen, based on intuition rather than proof.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, followed by a clause with or without *that*: *I have a feeling it's going to rain.* It sounds softer and more personal than *I think*, and it often introduces a prediction. *I had a feeling* is used when your guess turned out to be right.
examples: **I have a feeling** this is going to be a long night.
**I have a feeling that** we took a wrong turn; none of this looks familiar.
"They broke up." "Really? **I had a feeling** something was wrong."

drill.sentence: Look at those dark clouds. {{I have a feeling}} the game is going to be canceled.
drill.hint: my intuition says; four words (not *I bet*, *something tells me* or *… hunch*)

entries.related: *I have a hunch* — same, a bit more casual; *something tells me* — playful, based on small signs; *I bet* — more confident.

entries.label: hedging phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces what you think is probably true when you don't know for sure.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and meetings, followed by a clause, often with *that*. It sounds reasonable and honest about uncertainty. *My best guess is* suggests a careful estimate, for example of a number, a cost or a time.
examples: **My guess is** they'll raise the price again next year.
"Why's the dog barking?" "**My guess is** there's a squirrel in the yard."
**My best guess is** that the repairs will take about two weeks.

drill.sentence: I don't know why the store closed early, but {{my guess is}} the power went out.
drill.hint: I think it's probably the case that; three words (not *I bet* or *probably*)

entries.related: *I'd guess* — same, shorter; *I bet* — more confident, casual; *I'd imagine* — softer, thoughtful.

entries.label: hedging phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you suppose something is probably true, based on what you know, though you are not sure.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and polite discussion, followed by a clause: *I'd imagine it's expensive.* It is softer and more thoughtful than *I think*, and it often comments on other people's situations or feelings. *I imagine* means the same, and *I'd imagine so* is a common short reply.
entries.pattern: I'd imagine (that) + clause / I'd imagine so
examples: "Is parking hard downtown?" "**I'd imagine** it's a nightmare on game days."
**I'd imagine** your parents were pretty proud when you graduated.
With three teenagers in the house, **I'd imagine** your grocery bill is pretty high.

drill.sentence: "Is it hard to find a babysitter on New Year's Eve?" "{{I'd imagine}} it's almost impossible."
drill.hint: my reasonable assumption is; two words, with *would* (not *I'd guess* or *I'd say*)

entries.related: *I imagine* — same; *I'd guess* — a bit more casual; *I suppose* — similar, can sound reluctant.

entries.label: hedging phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces your impression or opinion, presenting it as the way things look to you rather than as a fact.
entries.usage: Common in discussions, meetings and thoughtful conversation, followed by a clause with or without *that*. It sounds measured and slightly formal, and it softens criticism: *It seems to me we're spending too much.* *Seems to me* without *it* is a casual spoken version.
examples: **It seems to me that** the kids are happier since we moved.
**It seems to me** we've been talking about this kitchen remodel for three years.
**It seems to me** the city should fix the potholes before it builds a new stadium.

drill.sentence: {{It seems to me}} you're working too hard. When was your last day off?
drill.hint: my impression is; four words (not *it looks like* or *I think*)

entries.related: *it looks to me like* — casual, based on what you see; *in my view* — more formal; *I get the impression that* — based on small signs.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces your opinion as it looks from your own position, experience or role.
entries.usage: Common at work, in meetings, interviews and serious conversations; it is a little more formal than *to me* or *in my opinion*. It often names your role: *from my perspective as a parent*. In casual chat it can sound a bit like business talk.
examples: **From my perspective**, the new schedule makes life harder for nurses on the night shift.
**From my perspective** as a teacher, the kids need more time outside.
I get why you're upset, but **from my perspective**, I was just trying to help.

drill.sentence: {{From my perspective}} as a renter, the new parking rules are a real headache.
drill.hint: seen from my position; three words (not *in my opinion* or *… point of view*)

entries.related: *from my point of view* — same, a bit plainer; *from where I'm standing* — casual, stresses your situation; *in my opinion* — neutral, general.

entries.term: if it were up to me
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces what you would decide if you had the power to choose, usually because someone else decides.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and at work when you don't agree with a decision but can't change it; the main clause uses *would* or *'d*. *If it was up to me* is also very common in speech. Both forms are fine in conversation, but careful writers prefer *were*.
entries.pattern: If it were up to me, + would + verb
examples: **If it were up to me**, we'd spend every vacation at the beach.
**If it were up to me**, you'd get the job, but the final decision is the owner's.
"Can we get a dog?" "**If it were up to me**, sure. Ask your mom."

drill.sentence: {{If it were up to me}}, the school day would start at nine, not seven-thirty.
drill.hint: if I could decide; six words (not *if I had my way*)

entries.related: *if I had my way* — same idea, stronger wish; *if I were in charge* — stresses power; *it's not up to me* — I can't decide this.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Signals that you are about to say something honest and direct, often critical or unwelcome.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, meetings and opinion writing, usually at the start of a sentence or after *and* or *but*. It sounds blunt and serious, more so than *honestly*, so it can suggest that you are annoyed. *Quite frankly* is stronger, and *to be frank* is a little more formal.
examples: **Frankly**, I don't think he deserves a second chance.
The service was slow and, **frankly**, the food wasn't worth the price.
"What did you think of my speech?" "**Frankly**? It was too long."

drill.sentence: I've asked you three times to clean the garage, and {{frankly}}, I'm getting tired of asking.
drill.hint: to be blunt and direct; one word (not *honestly* or *seriously*)

entries.related: *honestly* — softer, more common in casual speech; *to be frank* — a little more formal; *to be blunt* — even more direct.

entries.spoken_term: I'm not a hundred percent sure
entries.label: hedging phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you are fairly sure but not completely certain, so the listener may want to check.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, emails and texts, at work and in daily life; it is often followed by *but* and your best answer. It sounds friendly and honest, less formal than *I'm not certain*. People say *a hundred percent* or *one hundred percent*.
examples: **I'm not 100% sure**, but I think the pharmacy closes at nine.
"Is the party at Kate's or at her parents' house?" "**I'm not 100% sure**. Let me text her."
**I'm not 100% sure** this is the right bus, so I'm going to ask the driver.

drill.sentence: {{I'm not 100% sure}}, but I think the parade starts at ten on Saturday.
drill.hint: nearly but not completely certain; four words with a number (not *I'm not positive*)

entries.related: *I'm not positive* — same, casual; *I think so, but don't quote me* — joking, casual; *I'm not certain* — more neutral or formal.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: A polite *no* that shows regret when the answer is disappointing; *I'm afraid so* is the matching sad *yes*.
entries.usage: Common in customer service, at work and in polite conversation. *Afraid* here means *sorry*, not *scared*. It sounds polite and a little formal; with friends, *Sadly, no* or *Nope, sorry* is more casual.
examples: "Do you have this jacket in a large?" "**I'm afraid not**. We're sold out."
"Can I still change my flight for free?" "**I'm afraid not**, sir. There's a fifty-dollar fee."
"Is the hike really six hours?" "**I'm afraid so**. Bring plenty of water."

drill.sentence: "Is there any way to get tickets for tonight's show?" "{{I'm afraid not}}. It's been sold out for weeks."
drill.hint: a polite, regretful no; three words (not *sadly, no* or *unfortunately not*)

mistake.wrong: "Is the store still open?" "I'm afraid no."
mistake.right: "Is the store still open?" "I'm afraid not."
mistake.why: After *I'm afraid*, *I hope* and *I guess*, a short answer uses *not* for a no and *so* for a yes.

entries.related: *I'm afraid so* — a sad yes; *unfortunately not* — a bit more formal; *I'm sorry, no* — plain and polite.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: Says that nobody can know the answer, often about the future; it can sound hopeful or resigned.
entries.usage: Common in casual conversation as a rhetorical question, often with a shrug; no answer is expected. It can express real hope (*Who knows, maybe you'll win*) or simple uncertainty. Unlike *beats me*, which says that *you* don't know, *who knows?* says that nobody does.
examples: Will the house sell this summer? **Who knows?** The market's crazy right now.
Send the application anyway. **Who knows**, they might call you.
Maybe we'll move to Portugal one day. **Who knows?**

drill.sentence: I might stay in this town forever, or I might move to Japan next year. {{Who knows}}?
drill.hint: nobody can tell what will happen; two words (not *beats me* or *we'll see*)

entries.related: *beats me* — I personally have no idea; *we'll see* — wait for the result; *who can say?* — same, a bit more formal.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: A casual way to say *I have no idea*, especially about something puzzling.
entries.usage: Common in relaxed American conversation as a quick reply to a question, often with a shrug. It sounds a bit careless, so it doesn't fit formal situations or talk with clients. It can also come before a *why* clause: *Beats me why they closed the park.*
examples: "Where did Dad put the car keys?" "**Beats me**. Check his jacket."
"Why is there a goat in the neighbor's yard?" "**Beats me**."
**Beats me** why anyone would pay twenty bucks for a hot dog at a ballgame.

drill.sentence: "How does this coffee machine work?" "{{Beats me}}. I've never used it either."
drill.hint: casual American shrug: zero knowledge here; two words (not *no idea* or *search me*)

entries.related: *no idea* — neutral; *search me* — same, a bit old-fashioned; *who knows?* — nobody can know.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Says that a situation, especially a relationship, is too messy or difficult to explain simply.
entries.usage: Common in casual conversation as a reply to personal questions, and it often means *I don't want to explain*. Because it was a famous Facebook relationship status, it often hints at romantic or family trouble. Compared with *it's a long story*, it is about how messy the situation is, not how long the story would take.
examples: "So are you and Alex together now?" "**It's complicated**."
"Why don't you talk to your brother anymore?" "**It's complicated**. Maybe I'll tell you someday."
**It's complicated**: my ex and I still share the dog and the apartment lease.

drill.sentence: "Are you moving to Denver or not?" "{{It's complicated}}. It depends on my wife's job, our lease and about ten other things."
drill.hint: hard to explain in simple terms; two words (not *… tricky* or *long story*)

entries.related: *it's a long story* — the explanation would take too long; *don't ask* — the story is bad; *it's a bit tricky* — hard to deal with or explain.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: Says that you are happy with both of two options and don't mind which one is chosen.
entries.usage: Common when someone offers you a choice, in restaurants, stores and at home. It is polite and easygoing, but if the other person really wants your opinion, it can sound unhelpful, so people often add a small preference. For more than two options, say *Any of them is fine* or *Whatever's easiest*.
examples: "Coffee or tea?" "**Either one is fine**, thanks."
"Do you want the window seat or the aisle?" "Honestly, **either one is fine**."
We can meet Saturday or Sunday — **either one is fine** with me.

drill.sentence: "Should I bring red wine or white?" "{{Either one is fine}}. We're having pasta."
drill.hint: both options work for me; four words (not *… way …* or *I don't mind*)

entries.related: *either is fine* — same, shorter; *I don't mind* — neutral; *whichever* — casual, one word.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: Asks whether the listener now understands your point, usually right after an example or a piece of evidence.
entries.usage: Common in casual explanations and arguments, often right after something happens that proves your point. It can sound friendly or a little like *I told you so*. *You know what I mean?* is different: it is a filler that checks general understanding.
examples: Look how slow this line is moving. **See what I mean?** We should've come earlier.
"The dog just stole my sandwich!" "**See what I mean**? He's a thief."
Here, try this bread. **See what I mean**? It's way better than the store-bought kind.

drill.sentence: Watch: every time I open the door, the cat runs to the fridge. {{See what I mean}}?
drill.hint: do you understand my point now? four words (not *you know …* or *told you*)

entries.related: *told you* — casual, a bit smug; *you know what I mean?* — a filler; *get it?* — checks if someone understands a joke or idea.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces an explanation, especially one that the listener needs in order to understand a situation.
entries.usage: Common in storytelling and explanations, at the start of the explaining sentence. It can sound patient and friendly, but when overused it may seem a little like teaching. In casual speech, *see* alone is also common: *See, that's why I left.*
examples: I can't come tonight. **You see**, my car's been in the shop since Monday.
**You see**, when I was a kid, we didn't have a TV, so I read everything.
The bread didn't rise. **You see**, the yeast was way too old.

drill.sentence: I'm sorry the package is late. {{You see}}, our delivery van broke down on the highway.
drill.hint: introduces the explanation; two words (not *the thing is* or *actually*)

entries.related: *the thing is* — introduces a problem or reason; *see* — casual, same function; *you know* — a filler, not mainly for explanations.

entries.label: question tag
entries.meaning: An informal tag added to a statement to ask for agreement or to show surprise, like *right?* or *isn't it?*
entries.usage: Very common in casual American speech after a short statement: *Pretty cool, huh?* After surprising news it often sounds amused or skeptical: *So you're quitting, huh?* It is too casual for formal speech, and in some tones it sounds sarcastic.
examples: Nice weather we're having, **huh**? It finally feels like spring.
So you finally bought a car, **huh**? What kind?
Not bad for a first try, **huh**?

drill.sentence: So the new guy is your neighbor too, {{huh}}? Small world.
drill.hint: casual tag for agreement or amused surprise; one short sound (not *right* or *eh*)

entries.related: *right?* — checks agreement or facts; *eh?* — Canadian or British; *isn't it?* — standard question tag, more neutral.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces a side topic or an extra piece of information that is not the main point of the conversation.
entries.usage: Very common in speech, texts and emails, at the start or end of a sentence; in texts it is often *BTW*. It marks the new point as less important, though people sometimes use it to bring up something they care about a lot. It doesn't need to connect to the topic before it.
examples: **By the way**, your mom called while you were out.
Thanks for dinner! Oh, and **by the way**, I left my scarf on your chair.
The bus was twenty minutes late again, **by the way**.

drill.sentence: Great game last night. {{By the way}}, do you still need a ride to the airport on Friday?
drill.hint: introducing a side topic, casually; three words (not *anyway* or *on another note*)

entries.related: *incidentally* — more formal; *on another note* — moves to a new topic; *speaking of which* — picks up something just mentioned.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Returns to what you were talking about before you were interrupted or the conversation moved on.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, meetings, classes and talks after an interruption such as a phone call or a question. It sounds natural and polite, but with a pointed tone after a rude interruption it can show irritation. *Like I was saying* is very common in casual American speech.
examples: Sorry, I had to take that call. **As I was saying**, the contractor wants to start Monday.
**As I was saying** before the kids ran in, we really need a new car.
The teacher waited for the noise to stop and then said, "**As I was saying**, the test is next Thursday."

drill.sentence: Okay, the waiter's gone. {{As I was saying}}, I think we should split the check.
drill.hint: back to my point after the interruption; four words (not *anyway* or *like I …*)

entries.related: *like I was saying* — same, more casual; *anyway* — returns to the main topic; *where was I?* — when you've lost your place.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces a new topic that is different from the one you were discussing.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, meetings, emails and newsletters to move to an unrelated subject, often after a serious or sad one. It is a smooth, neutral way to change topics. *On a different note* means the same, while *on a related note* introduces a connected topic.
examples: That's all I have on the budget. **On another note**, who's bringing snacks to Friday's party?
Okay, enough about the broken dishwasher. **On another note**, how was your trip?
Anyway, I hope your dad feels better soon. **On another note**, are you still coming to Sam's birthday dinner?

drill.sentence: The kitchen repairs should be done by Friday. {{On another note}}, has anyone seen my black umbrella?
drill.hint: switching to an unrelated topic; three words (not *by the way* or *changing the subject*)

entries.related: *on a different note* — same; *on a related note* — a connected topic; *changing the subject* — openly announces a topic change.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Returns the conversation to an earlier topic after a side discussion.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, interviews, classes and conversation, followed by the topic: *Getting back to the budget, …* It sounds organized and polite, and it is useful when a discussion has moved away from its main point. *Back to* + topic is a shorter, more casual version.
examples: Okay, **getting back to** your question about the car, I think you should sell it.
That's a funny story, but **getting back to** the wedding plans, we still need a photographer.
**Getting back to** what we talked about yesterday, I've decided to take the job.

drill.sentence: Anyway, enough about my neighbor's dog. {{Getting back to}} your trip, where are you staying in Chicago?
drill.hint: returning to the earlier subject; three words, -ing form (not *going …* or *coming …*)

entries.related: *back to* + topic — short, casual; *as I was saying* — returns to your own interrupted point; *anyway* — returns to the main topic.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you have talked about yourself long enough and now want to hear about the other person.
entries.usage: Common in friendly conversation, often with a little laugh and followed by a question like *How are you?* It sounds polite and self-aware, because it shows interest in the other person. A well-known joke turns it around: *But enough about me — what do you think of me?*
examples: Anyway, that's my crazy week. **Enough about me** — how's the new job?
But **enough about me**. How are your parents doing?
After twenty minutes about his fishing trip, Greg finally said, "Okay, **enough about me**."

drill.sentence: Sorry, I've been talking about my wedding plans all night. {{Enough about me}}. How's school going?
drill.hint: let's talk about you now; three words (not *anyway*)

entries.related: *but what about you?* — turns the question back; *I've been going on and on* — admits you talked too much; *anyway* — closes your topic.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Adds another reason or argument, often the stronger or more personal one, to support what you have just said.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and informal writing at the start of a sentence, often to support a refusal or a decision, so it can sound a little like an excuse. As a preposition, *besides* also means *in addition to*: *Who's coming besides Tom?*
examples: I don't need a new phone. **Besides**, this one works fine.
Let's stay in tonight. It's freezing out. **Besides**, I'm broke until payday.
"Why didn't you apply for the manager job?" "I like what I do. **Besides**, the hours are terrible."

drill.sentence: I'm too tired to go to the gym. {{Besides}}, it's already nine o'clock.
drill.hint: and another reason is; one word (not *plus*, *also* or *anyway*)

mistake.why: *Beside* without *s* means *next to*; the linking word that adds a reason is *besides*.

entries.related: *plus* — casual, adds a point; *anyway* — dismisses the previous point; *what's more* — a bit more formal, adds a stronger point.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: An informal way to add another point or reason, meaning *and also* or *in addition*.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech and texts, at the start of a sentence or in the middle after a comma. It usually adds another reason or advantage to an argument. In formal writing, *in addition* or *also* is safer, because some editors don't accept *plus* as a linking word.
examples: I love this neighborhood. It's quiet. **Plus**, there's a great bakery on the corner.
Take the train. It's faster, **plus** you can read on the way.
"Why did you pick this gym?" "It's cheap. **Plus**, they have a pool."

drill.sentence: The hotel's right on the beach. {{Plus}}, breakfast is included in the price.
drill.hint: and also, in a casual style; one word (not *besides* or *also*)

entries.related: *also* — neutral; *besides* — adds a reason, often for a refusal; *on top of that* — casual, often adds a problem.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces a point that remains true despite what was just said: *even so*.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing, at the start of a sentence that follows a concession. It often sounds a little reluctant or thoughtful. In speech, *but still* at the end of a sentence is very common, meaning the problem remains: *I know he apologized, but still.*
examples: The hotel was a little far from the center. **Still**, we had a great time.
I know it was an accident. **Still**, you should apologize to her.
"He said he was sorry." "I know, but **still**."

drill.sentence: The concert tickets cost way too much. {{Still}}, it was the best show I've ever seen.
drill.hint: despite that; one word (not *however* or *anyway*)

entries.related: *even so* — a bit stronger; *anyway* — casual, the first point doesn't matter; *however* — more formal, mostly written.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces a point that is true despite what was just said, often one that is surprising given the first fact.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing, at the start of a sentence or after *but*. It sounds slightly more formal and emphatic than *still*. It usually follows a fact that would make the next point seem unlikely.
examples: We left two hours early. **Even so**, we almost missed the flight.
The movie got terrible reviews, but **even so**, it made a lot of money.
She's been driving for thirty years. **Even so**, she hates parking downtown.

drill.sentence: I studied the driver's manual every night for a week, but {{even so}}, I failed the written test.
drill.hint: despite that; two words (not *still* or *all the same*)

entries.related: *still* — very similar, more common in casual speech; *all the same* — same meaning; *nevertheless* — formal, mostly written.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces one positive point in a bad or disappointing situation.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation when you comfort someone or yourself, usually at the start of a sentence or after *but*. In this sense it has nothing to do with numbers (*at least ten people*); it points to something good.
examples: The flight was delayed for hours, but **at least** they gave us free food.
"I didn't get the job." "I'm sorry. **At least** you got some good interview practice."
My phone fell in the pool. **At least** it was an old one.

drill.sentence: Our power was out all weekend, but {{at least}} the food in the freezer stayed cold.
drill.hint: the one small consolation is that; two words (not *luckily* or *thankfully*)

entries.related: *on the bright side* — the good part, a bit more cheerful; *luckily* — by good luck; *thank goodness* — relief.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces the good part of a situation that is mostly bad.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, texts and light writing, often after a complaint, to cheer yourself or someone else up. It sounds positive and often humorous. *Look on the bright side* is advice to stay positive.
examples: The game got rained out. **On the bright side**, we got to sleep in.
"I broke my leg." "Oh no! **On the bright side**, you can finally finish that book."
I know the house is a mess, but **look on the bright side**: the kids are learning to cook.

drill.sentence: Our flight was canceled. {{On the bright side}}, we get one more night at the beach.
drill.hint: seeing the good part of it; four words (not *on the plus …* or *at least*)

entries.related: *on the plus side* — same; *at least* — one small good point; *every cloud has a silver lining* — a proverb with the same idea.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Adds a detail that is surprising or that corrects what the other person thought; similar to *actually*.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, at the start or end of a sentence, and a little emphatic. It often answers a doubtful question with a surprising answer, so it can sound proud or slightly defensive. *Actually* is shorter and more frequent, and *in fact* is more common in writing.
examples: "Have you ever been to Alaska?" "**As a matter of fact**, I lived there for three years."
"You don't know how to cook, do you?" "**As a matter of fact**, I made this whole dinner myself."
I don't mind the rain. **As a matter of fact**, I kind of like it.

drill.sentence: "I bet you've never ridden a horse." "{{As a matter of fact}}, I grew up on a ranch."
drill.hint: contrary to what you think; five words (not *actually*)

entries.related: *actually* — shorter, very common; *in fact* — more common in writing; *believe it or not* — stresses that the fact is surprising.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces a new person or thing that you now want to talk about, often in contrast to the one before.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing at the start of a sentence, to move to the next item in a list of topics. It often marks a contrast. *As for me* is a very common way to give your own position after describing other people's.
examples: Mom's flying in on Friday. **As for** Dad, he's driving up on Sunday.
The pasta was great. **As for** the dessert, I wouldn't order it again.
My friends all moved to the suburbs. **As for me**, I'm staying in the city.

drill.sentence: The hotel room was lovely. {{As for}} the breakfast, it was cold and overpriced.
drill.hint: now turning to; two words (not *as to* or *regarding*)

entries.related: *regarding* — more formal, often in writing; *when it comes to* — introduces a topic area; *as to* — formal, mostly before *whether*.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Signals that the words you just used are not exact or literal, but a figurative way of putting it.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing, usually right after the figurative words. It shows that you know the expression is unusual, playful or a bit imprecise. It sounds educated but not stiff, while *if you will* is more formal.
examples: Grandpa was the glue that held our family together, **so to speak**.
We're finally in the home stretch, **so to speak** — the kitchen's almost done.
The new coach will have to clean house, **so to speak**, before the season starts.

drill.sentence: My little brother is the black sheep of the family, {{so to speak}}. He's the only one who didn't go to college.
drill.hint: if you allow the figurative words; three words (not *if you will*, *in a way* or *in a sense*)

entries.related: *if you will* — more formal; *in a manner of speaking* — same, a bit literary; *in a way* — partly true, not about word choice.

entries.label: filler
entries.meaning: An informal way to end a story or explanation when you have nothing more to add.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech, especially among younger speakers, after a story or an update, often with a falling voice and a pause. It signals that you're done and gives the turn to the listener. It sounds vague and unpolished, so avoid it in presentations and interviews.
examples: And then the vet said Max needs surgery, which isn't cheap. **So yeah**.
I didn't get the scholarship, but I'm going to apply again next year. **So yeah**.
"How was the date?" "He was nice, but he talked about his ex the whole time. **So yeah**."

drill.sentence: Anyway, the car's in the shop and I'm taking the bus all week. {{So yeah}}. How about you?
drill.hint: a casual way to wrap up what I was saying; two words (not *that's it* or *so anyway*)

entries.related: *that's about it* — neutral, nothing more to add; *anyway* — closes a topic; *long story short* — introduces a quick summary.

entries.label: vague language
entries.meaning: A vague ending to a list, meaning *and other similar things*.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech and texts, especially among younger people. It sounds relaxed but vague, and using it a lot can sound childish or careless. *And things like that* is more neutral, and *and so on* is more formal.
examples: We just hung out, played video games **and stuff**.
I need to buy shampoo, sunscreen **and stuff** for the trip.
She's really into hiking, camping **and stuff** like that.

drill.sentence: This weekend I'm just going to clean the house, do laundry {{and stuff}}.
drill.hint: and similar chores, said vaguely; two words (not *and things* or *and all*)

entries.related: *and things like that* — neutral; *and so on* — more formal; *or whatever* — vague, can sound careless.

entries.label: spoken reply
entries.meaning: A dismissive reply meaning *I don't care* or *I'm not going to argue*, often showing annoyance.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech, especially in arguments with family or friends, and teenagers are famous for it. With a flat tone or an eye roll it sounds rude and childish, as if you refuse to discuss. In *Whatever you want*, with a relaxed tone, it simply means you're easygoing.
examples: "You need to clean your room before dinner." "**Whatever**."
"I still think you're wrong." "**Whatever**, I'm done arguing about it."
Every time I try to talk to my brother about money, he just says "**whatever**" and leaves the room.

drill.sentence: "You're not allowed to use the car this weekend." "{{Whatever}}. I didn't want to go anywhere anyway."
drill.hint: dismissive: I don't care; one word (not *fine* or *okay*)

entries.related: *fine* — can also sound annoyed; *I don't care* — more direct; *suit yourself* — do what you want.

entries.label: softener
entries.meaning: Added after a request or plan to ask politely whether the other person agrees with it.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, emails and texts with colleagues, hosts, neighbors and family. It makes a request or plan sound less demanding, though often the speaker has already decided. *If that works for you* is common for times and plans, and *if you don't mind* is similar.
examples: I'm going to bring my sister to the party, **if that's OK with you**.
I'd rather sit by the window, **if that's OK**.
I'll pay you back next week, **if that's OK**. My paycheck comes on Friday.

drill.sentence: We'll come by around seven, {{if that's OK with you}}.
drill.hint: asking politely for your agreement; five words (not *if you don't mind* or *… works for you*)

entries.related: *if that works for you* — for times and plans; *if you don't mind* — similar; *is that OK?* — a direct question.

entries.label: softener
entries.meaning: Added before or after a suggestion to make it sound modest, so that the listener feels free to reject it.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, meetings and informal emails, before or after the suggestion. It sounds friendly and humble. After a pointed suggestion (*Maybe call your mother?*), it can be gently sarcastic.
examples: **Just a thought**, but what if we had the party in the backyard?
Maybe we could take the train instead of driving? **Just a thought**.
Her email ended with "**Just a thought** — feel free to ignore it."

drill.sentence: We could invite the new neighbors to the barbecue. {{Just a thought}}.
drill.hint: only a suggestion, no pressure; three words (not *… an idea* or *… saying*)

entries.related: *just an idea* — same; *just saying* — adds a point, often a bit critical; *what if we …?* — the suggestion itself.
